text:
## Observations

1. The optimum equals the minimum, over sequences of adjacent swaps, of the swap count plus the number of equal-value runs in the resulting array.
2. Group neighboring blocks of swapped positions together. Each such group can save at most one operation compared with deleting the original runs, and a group that saves one must have an untouched position on each side.
3. Every group that saves one operation can be replaced by a chain of consecutive, disjoint swaps of adjacent pairs between two untouched positions.
4. A valid chain changes every originally unequal adjacency between its two untouched endpoints into an equal adjacency, except for the adjacencies inside its swapped pairs.
5. Chains can be combined when their intervals are disjoint or share only an untouched endpoint. For a fixed left endpoint, the earliest possible right endpoint leaves the most room for later chains.

## Solution sketch

> The optimum equals the minimum, over sequences of adjacent swaps, of the swap count plus the number of equal-value runs in the resulting array.

1. Count the original runs, denoting their number by \(R\). To see why it suffices to consider swaps followed by deletions, replay any strategy while keeping deleted prefixes frozen in place. Each swap still acts on adjacent positions of the unfrozen suffix. At the end, the replayed array is a concatenation of the homogeneous prefixes that the strategy deleted, so its run count is at most the strategy’s deletion count. Conversely, after any sequence of swaps, one deletion per resulting run empties the array.

> Group neighboring blocks of swapped positions together. Each such group can save at most one operation compared with deleting the original runs, and a group that saves one must have an untouched position on each side.

2. In an optimal swap sequence, join two adjacent positions if a swap uses the cut between them. The connected blocks of size at least two are the swapped blocks. A block of length \(L\) uses at least \(L-1\) swaps and initially has at most \(L-1\) unequal internal adjacencies. The block contains at least two distinct values, since swaps in a constant block can be omitted, so it still has at least one unequal internal adjacency at the end. The swap cost therefore exceeds the decrease in internal unequal adjacencies by at least one per block. A group of \(k\) neighboring swapped blocks has at most \(k+1\) other adjacencies it can improve, counting the boundaries between blocks and the two outer boundaries. Each can save at most one operation. Thus the group saves at most one overall, and reaching that bound requires both outer boundaries, every boundary changing from unequal to equal, and every block attaining equality in the internal count. Groups have disjoint sets of affected adjacencies, so groups with zero or negative savings can be omitted.

> Every group that saves one operation can be replaced by a chain of consecutive, disjoint swaps of adjacent pairs between two untouched positions.

3. In a group that saves one, every block starts with all its internal adjacencies unequal and ends with exactly one unequal internal adjacency. It therefore contains exactly two values and originally alternates between them. A block of length three would require two swaps to attain equality in the count from step 2, but either possible final order with two runs can be reached in one swap. This contradicts optimality. If any block has length at least four, take four consecutive positions within it. Swapping the middle two changes \(x,y,x,y\) into \(x,x,y,y\), removing two unequal adjacencies at a cost of one. That single swap can replace the whole group for the same saving. In all other cases, the blocks already consist of consecutive pairs, each swapped once.

> A valid chain changes every originally unequal adjacency between its two untouched endpoints into an equal adjacency, except for the adjacencies inside its swapped pairs.

4. Using one-based indices, compute from right to left the earliest right endpoint for a chain whose first swapped pair starts at \(i\). In this computation, defer the check on the boundary to the left of the pair. A pair is usable only if \(A_i\ne A_{i+1}\). It can end the chain at \(i+2\) if that position exists and \(A_i=A_{i+2}\). This makes the original right boundary unequal and the swapped boundary equal. Otherwise, it can continue with the pair starting at \(i+2\) if that pair exists, \(A_{i+1}\ne A_{i+2}\), and \(A_i=A_{i+3}\). The first comparison checks the original boundary and the second checks it after both pairs are swapped. Inherit the earliest endpoint already computed for \(i+2\). If neither option yields an endpoint, record that none exists. To start a chain at an untouched left endpoint \(\ell\), use the pair starting at \(\ell+1\) and also require \(A_\ell=A_{\ell+2}\). With \(k\) swapped pairs, the chain removes \(k+1\) unequal adjacencies in \(k\) swaps, saving exactly one operation.

> Chains can be combined when their intervals are disjoint or share only an untouched endpoint. For a fixed left endpoint, the earliest possible right endpoint leaves the most room for later chains.

5. Compute a second right-to-left dynamic program. At position \(\ell\), store the maximum number of compatible chains with left endpoints at or after \(\ell\). Either skip \(\ell\) and use the value for \(\ell+1\), or start a valid chain there with earliest right endpoint \(r\) and take one plus the value for \(r\). Using the value for \(r\) allows the next chain to share that untouched endpoint. A later right endpoint can only restrict the available suffix, so testing the earliest one suffices. Initialize the value beyond the array to zero and treat out-of-range pairs or endpoints as unavailable. Print \(R\) minus the value at position \(1\) for each test case. An all-equal array has one run and no valid chain, and an array of distinct values has \(N\) runs and no valid chain. The algorithm takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(N)\) space per case, with \(O(\sum N)\) total time.
system_prompt:
You are a programming problem planner. Produce a natural-language guide
with exactly these headings:
## Observations
Give numbered, useful observations derived from the problem specification.
## Solution sketch
Describe one coherent algorithm as numbered steps. Before each step quote the
relevant observation exactly, then explain how that observation supports the step.
Cover edge cases and time/space complexity in the sketch.
Return prose only, without Python implementation or command blocks.
The guide will be implemented by a separate coding agent.

generation.note: Harness wall time includes Codex startup; not API latency.

usage.note: Codex token counts include its harness context; not comparable to API usage.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
